newsitem.title: UK: WEEK AHEAD - U.S. data to keep markets enthralled.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - U.S. data to keep markets enthralled.

text.p: Financial markets will focus on the twists and turns of the U.S. economy in the coming week as another batch of key figures arrives, economists said on Friday.

U.S. producer prices, retail sales and the Federal Reserve's "Beige Book" will dominate as markets assess whether the economy is expanding too fast for comfort. In Europe, British producer price and industrial production numbers are due. Also, there is talk of an interest rate rise in the Netherlands. After U.S. employment numbers on Friday, which left the debate over the timing of any Fed policy decision still finely balanced, the spotlight was clearly on the trend-setting U.S. Nonfarm payrolls in February rose 339,000, well above expectations, but wage pressures did not look too severe, analysts said. "The money markets are certain there will be a rate hike at some point but they're not certain of the timing, so I still think we have a lot of indecision out there," said Brian Venables, senior bond analyst at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett in Amsterdam.

The Fed's Beige Book on economic conditions is due on Wednesday, followed by U.S. retail sales for February on Thursday and producer prices on Friday. Nonetheless, market anxiety will not be as heightened after the past week. "For the U.S. it's pretty much just consolidation. All the news is out there now," said Graham McDevitt, senior analyst at Paribas Capital Markets in London. "Greenspan has spoken, the employment report has happened," he said. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan completed semi-annual congressional testimony in the past week. "To me the question is, Does the Fed deliver on March 25 or does it delay," McDevitt said, referring to the next Fed policy setting meeting. "People are still going to be nervous about whether the Fed's going to pull the trigger," said George Magnus, chief international economist at UBS in London. "I think it will remain tense."

He said the equity market would try to maintain its bullish stance right up until a Fed rate move looks imminent. "Probably the equity market is going to keep going until it sees the whites of the eyes of a tightening," "The bond market is going to remain in a holding pattern,' he said, although it had a negative tilt. But while bond and stock markets have been nervous amid uncertainty over policy, the dollar has been buoyant. Analysts said its strength will continue to be in the spotlight for many other markets.

"The dollar's a big factor for Europe. It's been a factor which has helped the European currencies (against the mark) and also the European spreads claw back from their worst levels last week," McDevitt said.

Elsewhere there is growing talk that the Dutch central bank might decide to increase interest rates again, analysts said. "We think it's possible the Dutch will hike again," Venables said. He noted a recent tightening had failed to bolster the guilder against the mark, which he said had been the central bank's aim.

The guilder/mark cross had been suffering partly because any safe-haven flows into the mark were not being matched in the guilder, analysts said. That was because 10-year debt spreads still showed a narrow premium for German yields over Dutch, they added.
A number of Japanese numbers are due next week, although until the Japanese "Tankan" survey is out in April, analysts said the market was unlikely to see drastic activity.
Japanese wholesale prices for February are due on Monday followed by machinery orders on Tuesday. Fourth-quarter gross domestic product is due any time from Friday.
